checkpoints: Server and Client components run in different runtimes at different times, and the serialized RSC payload is the only bridge between them.
Because a client island's props travel inside that payload (encoded server-side, decoded in the browser), they must be plain data — strings, numbers, plain structures — not live references.
A closure carries its own live scope and identity, which cannot be serialized, so passing an inline function like onAdded triggers an immediate serialization error at render.

The fix is to keep behavior inside the Client Component itself (pass only data down and define the handler there), or pass a server-function reference that serializes into a callable id instead of a plain closure.

Composition only flows one way: a Server Component can render a Client Component, but a Client Component can never import a Server Component, because by the time client code runs the server render has already finished and there's no environment left to execute it.

The ThemeProvider paradox resolves via the children pattern: the parent Server Component renders its server content first, then hands the already-finished output into ThemeProvider as a children slot.

ThemeProvider never re-executes that content — it just places the pre-rendered slot inside its own output, which is exactly how an app-wide client provider coexists with zero-JS server pages inside it.

Partial prerendering moves the static-vs-dynamic decision from the whole route down to the region inside or outside a Suspense boundary — a build-time static shell combined with request-time dynamic holes, delivered in one streamed HTTP response.
Fully static generation paints instantly from a CDN but cannot serve the cart badge at all, since a fully static build has no per-request state.
force-dynamic fixes the personalization but overcorrects: the unchanging title and description now also wait on a server render on every request, delaying first byte.

A static shell with client-side fetch paints the shell fast and fetches the badge after hydration, but requires a second request the browser only discovers after JS runs, ships extra fetching logic as JS, and leaves a visibly empty hole or skeleton until that request resolves.
At build time, partial prerendering prerenders everything reading no request-time signal — including the Suspense fallback skeleton itself — into the static shell.

Anything reading cookies/headers/an uncached fetch inside a Suspense boundary is deferred and streamed into that exact placeholder slot at request time, over the same connection as the shell — no second request, no client-fetch waterfall.

What makes PPR materially different from a static shell plus client-side fetch is the single-response property: one connection carries both layers, versus a request that exists only because client JavaScript decided to make it.

The discipline PPR demands and its production hesitations: a request-time read placed outside any Suspense boundary silently makes the whole route dynamic (the shell disappears with no error); plus the feature is experimental and pinned to canary builds, the per-route experimental_ppr flag fails silently as a no-op if forgotten, and data baked into the shell at build time is frozen until the next rebuild or revalidation.
The crash is not the async Server Component's await nor the island's own useState — it's the inline onAdded={() => console.log(...)} prop passed where page.tsx renders <AddToCartButton>.

Because AddToCartButton is 'use client', every prop passed into it must survive the trip from server render to browser: React encodes the Server Component's output, including the Client Component's props, into the RSC payload that the browser decodes.

Plain data like the productId string survives that trip fine, but the onAdded closure captures live server scope (product.name) that cannot be serialized, so React throws immediately with 'Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components.'
The general rule this illustrates: data crosses the server/client boundary, behavior does not.
The fix is to delete the onAdded prop and define the handler inside AddToCartButton itself, since it already receives productId and the interaction logic belongs entirely inside the client island.

If the behavior genuinely must execute on the server (e.g. writing an analytics row), pass a 'use server' Server Function reference instead of a plain closure, since the framework serializes that into a callable id the client can invoke.
To verify the client fix: reload the page and confirm the serialization error is gone, then click 'Add to cart' and confirm the counter still increments, proving the island hydrates correctly.

To verify nothing else broke: View Page Source and confirm the product name/price still render as real server HTML, proving the fix only touched the client island's prop surface, not the zero-JS server part of the page.
This incident is actually two independent bugs stacking on top of each other, not one.

The root bug: DashboardPage is async with await getSummary() as its very first line, sitting above all the JSX and all three Suspense boundaries, so React can't emit anything — not even the shell or fallback skeletons — until that promise resolves, because the component itself hasn't finished returning.

This is the top-level-await-defeats-streaming failure mode: Suspense only splits the stream for an await that lives inside a boundary's child, not for an await sitting in the body of the page component that hosts the boundary, so TTFB carries the full ~1200ms and the skeletons never get a chance to appear.

The fix for the root bug is to keep page.tsx synchronous with no page-level await, pushing getSummary() into its own async child wrapped in its own Suspense boundary, so the Quick/Medium/Slow boundaries can then run in parallel with the summary.

The second, independent bug: inside Slow, await getUser() runs before await getRecommendations() even though recommendations doesn't depend on user, so the two independent calls sum sequentially (~1000ms) instead of running in parallel (~600ms max) — a hidden waterfall.
The fix for the second bug is to start both promises before awaiting either one and then Promise.all them, or to split user and recommendations into two separate sibling boundaries.
Verifying the root-bug fix: with network throttling on, the shell — with all three skeletons — should appear almost instantly instead of after the full ~1200ms.
Verifying the second-bug fix: the Slow widget should resolve at ~600ms (max) instead of ~1000ms (sum), and each widget should reveal in an order matching its own source's latency.

Blocker 1 — no server-side validation: `body.trim().length === 0` is a client-side UX nicety, not a security boundary; the route handler pushes `body` into the store with no re-check, so a direct POST bypasses the empty-check completely.

Fix for blocker 1: move validation into the mutation itself, parsing the submitted field with a schema (e.g. Zod) server-side, and return `{ error }` on failure rather than throwing — throwing would skip the form and hit the error boundary instead of rendering the message inline.
Blocker 2 — hydration dependency: `e.preventDefault()` + `fetch` makes the form entirely dependent on JavaScript having loaded and hydrated.
Fix for blocker 2: bind a `"use server"` action directly to the form's `action` attribute, so a real HTML POST still works even before hydration.
That restructure lets the hand-rolled state go: `useFormState` threads the action's returned state back into the UI in place of manual `isSubmitting`/`error` `useState`.
`useFormStatus` — read inside a child `Submit` component since it only sees the enclosing form's pending flag — replaces the manual disabled/"Posting..." toggle.

Lower severity: swap `router.refresh()` for `revalidatePath("/comments")` called inside the action itself (declarative/surgical vs a blunt whole-route re-fetch) — and once the action is in place, the `/api/comments` route handler and its `fetch`/JSON plumbing become dead code for this in-app form (keep a route only if an external client genuinely needs one).

Verify: a direct POST with an empty body is rejected server-side; an e2e pass with JavaScript disabled still submits the form and the comment appears; an empty submit renders "Required" inline with the comment count unchanged.

A static `import` is a compile-time edge in the dependency graph, so the bundler must ship that module in the initial chunk — every user downloads, parses, and compiles it before interacting, even if they never see the widget.
`lazy(() => import("./Heavy"))` replaces that static edge with a runtime `import()` expression — a deferred, on-demand reference instead of a compile-time one.
Rollup treats the dynamic `import()` as a split point and emits the module as its own hashed chunk.
React only fetches that chunk over the network when the lazy component actually mounts.
While the chunk is in flight, React suspends that subtree and renders the nearest `<Suspense fallback>`; once the chunk resolves, the real component swaps in.
Rendering a lazy component with no `Suspense` boundary above it makes React throw.
Net win in the lesson demo: the initial chunk drops from ~250 KB to ~50-80 KB, freeing the main thread earlier (better LCP, INP).
Trade-off: a one-time network round-trip when the widget first appears — exactly the gap the `Suspense` fallback bridges.
The freeze comes from a long task running on the browser's ONE single main thread — the exact thread also responsible for JS, layout, paint, and input handlers.

`setTimeout` is deferring, not offloading: it reschedules WHEN the parse starts, but the moment it starts, the same synchronous CPU-bound code still blocks every paint and every click until it finishes — so INP stays just as bad, no matter how much later it kicks off.

The structurally correct fix is a Web Worker: a genuine second OS thread with its own event loop (and no DOM), so that same parse runs in parallel while the main thread stays free to paint and handle input.
Exactly as the lesson demonstrates: Ping stays under 100ms while the worker parses 200,000 rows, while parsing the same amount of data on the main thread freezes the whole UI.

The price you pay is the boundary between the two threads: there's no shared writable memory, so everything has to cross via message passing, plus the cost of spawning the worker and serializing every message.

This is exactly why you only offload substantial CPU-bound work (large file parsing, image processing), not a computation of a few milliseconds, where the round-trip itself costs more than the compute.
Four defects, ranked by severity — this PR should not merge as-is.

Production breaker: `new Worker("./csv.worker.js")` passes a string path, which is not statically analyzable, so Vite never emits the worker chunk and it 404s right after build; the fix is `new Worker(new URL("./csv.worker.ts", import.meta.url), { type: "module" })` — the shape Vite recognizes and emits as its own fingerprinted chunk, while also making it a module worker able to `import` PapaParse/Comlink, keeping the main bundle small.

Lifecycle defect: creating a new worker on every click re-pays spawn cost repeatedly and leaks threads since nothing calls `terminate()`; it should be created once on mount (returning `{ api, raw }`) and `terminate()` called on `raw` during unmount.

Throughput defect: 10,000 awaited `api.processRow(row)` calls each pay serialization plus a round-trip — Comlink's ergonomics hide that this is cross-thread I/O; the whole loop should collapse into ONE worker method that takes the entire dataset.
Return-path defect: the large `ArrayBuffer` returned plainly gets structured-cloned; it should return through `Comlink.transfer` with a worker-owned buffer to move zero-copy.

Evidence bar: only a Performance recording showing the parse on the Worker track (Main clear), responsiveness (Ping/INP) during the parse, and the worker chunk visible in Network turns "it'll probably be faster" into proof — this PR has none of that.

Measure first, and root cause 1: a Profiler recording shows `ExpensiveList` re-rendering on every commit (Performance panel: ~10-30ms long tasks per counter click), because the filter+sort over 1,000 items sits at the top of the render function with no memoization tying it to `query`, so it re-runs even when `query` hasn't changed.
Root cause 2: `filtered` and the inline `onSelect` handler are fresh references on every render, so even a memoized child would still see "changed" props and re-render the entire 1,000-row subtree.
Fix (1): `useMemo(() => ITEMS.filter(...).sort(...), [query])` — recomputes only when `query` changes and returns the same reference otherwise.
Fix (2): `useCallback((id) => setSelectedId(id), [])` gives `onSelect` a stable reference.
Fix (3): wrap `ExpensiveList` and each `Row` in `React.memo` so the now-stable reference chain gives React an actual basis to skip the render.

Deps discipline: a missing dep leaves a stale value trapped in the closure (stale closure bug), an extra dep means the cache never hits since the input effectively "changes" every call; use `setCount(c => c + 1)` so `count` never needs to appear in any deps array, and turn on `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` so a missing dep is caught automatically.

Heuristic: this is worth doing precisely because the computation and subtree are genuinely large — not a case for blanket-wrapping every cheap component in `React.memo`, where the props-comparison cost can exceed the render it's meant to avoid.

Verify with the Profiler: after optimizing, clicking the counter shows `ExpensiveList` "Did not render", the Performance panel goes flat instead of spiking with long tasks, and a behavior check confirms typing still filters correctly and clicking a row still selects correctly.
Recognizes that the table is already virtualized and working — the regression comes from two independently mis-set parameters, not from missing virtualization.

Identifies overscan: 100 as too high: with a 600px viewport and ~48px rows, ~13 rows are visible plus a 2×100 buffer on each side, so 200+ real DOM nodes stay mounted every scroll frame — close to the cost of a naive full render.

States the overscan trade-off correctly (smoother fling-scroll / fewer blank flashes vs. more mounted nodes) and recommends bringing it down to the practical band ~3-10, which returns the DOM window to ~20-30 nodes.
Identifies estimateSize: () => 300 as mismatched against the real ~48px average row height.
Explains the mechanism: in dynamic mode the estimate sizes every unmeasured row, so getTotalSize() overestimates ~6x and keeps shrinking as each measureElement correction lands.
Connects that mechanism to the observed symptom: the scrollbar's length/position jumps or jitters during fast scroll as corrections settle.

Prescribes the fix — set estimateSize near the measured average (~48) so the scrollbar is proportional from the start — and gives a concrete verification (DOM node count before/after in DevTools, and/or FPS or scrollTop stability sampled during fast scroll).
States the general invariant being protected: mount/scroll cost should stay constant in viewport size, never scale with total data size.
